claim: The surah opens with a one-word oath, wa-l-ʿaṣr, swearing by al-ʿaṣr.
Here wa is an oath particle rather than a conjunction joining two things, and the noun after it is therefore in the genitive.
Verse 103:1 does not state what the oath concerns; the proposition is deferred to the next verse, which says that the human being is indeed in loss.
The first verse works as a threshold: the reader hears what is sworn by before knowing the judgment that will follow.
The oath is placed immediately beside the judgment about human loss, so hearing what al-ʿaṣr means also helps the reader hear what kind of loss is meant.
Elsewhere the Qurʾan swears by times of day: dawn, forenoon, night as it covers, and morning as it brightens.
Most of these time oaths pair the time with an action or change, such as night covering things or morning becoming bright.
In 103:1 al-ʿaṣr appears alone, without a modifier, leaving the word’s breadth open.
The root’s dictionary senses include both a long span or era and the part of the day near evening.
The afternoon prayer, ṣalāt al-ʿaṣr, takes its name from that time of day.
The definite article in al-ʿaṣr points to a known time, but the verse does not say whether it means the afternoon, the age in which a person lives, or time itself.
The single word leaves the reader to hear its possible senses together.
Turkish divides the word’s range: asır means a hundred years and asri means contemporary, while the late-day period is called ikindi.
In Turkish, asır does not evoke the fading evening light or the root’s other images of squeezing, refuge, and a whirlwind.
The word in the verse holds the day’s ending and an era together, so the end of a day and the end of a life bear the same name.
Arabic usage calls night and day together al-ʿaṣrān, or the two ʿaṣrs.
The same dual expression, al-ʿaṣrān, can also mean early morning and evening.
In 6:52 the Prophet is told not to drive away those who call on their Lord morning and evening while seeking His countenance.
terms: وَلَا تَطْرُدِ ٱلَّذِينَ يَدْعُونَ رَبَّهُم بِٱلْغَدَوٰةِ وَٱلْعَشِىِّ يُرِيدُونَ وَجْهَهُۥ

claim: In 11:114 the Prophet is commanded to establish prayer at the two ends of the day and in the early parts of the night.
terms: وَأَقِمِ ٱلصَّلَوٰةَ طَرَفَىِ ٱلنَّهَارِ وَزُلَفًۭا مِّنَ ٱلَّيْلِ

claim: Because ʿaṣr can name the day’s two edges, the word presents time from its boundaries, where a period begins and ends.
The afternoon sense of al-ʿaṣr is one of those edges: the day’s closing end.
The word can carry the sense of delay: the phrase jāʾanī fulān ʿaṣran describes someone arriving late and slowly.
The expression nāma wa-mā nāma li-ʿaṣr is used of someone who slept but did not sleep even for a moment.
A short span of time can be called al-ʿaṣār or al-ḥīn.
The root can thus name both a long era and a fleeting moment, and both an ordinary part of the day and the time of a delayed arrival.
The same word marks stages of life: a young woman may reach her youth and maturity, and a person’s lifespan and old age are also named with this word.
Late afternoon is the time when least of the day remains: work is nearly finished, light is waning, and time is short for what has not been done.
Al-ʿaṣr therefore means more than an hour; it carries the feeling of having come late within that hour.
The Qurʾanic examples portray time at its end as compressed and as a span measured retrospectively.
In 79:42 people ask the Prophet about the Hour and when its appointed time will be.
In 79:46, when people see the Hour, their whole stay seems to them no longer than an evening or its forenoon.
terms: كَأَنَّهُمْ يَوْمَ يَرَوْنَهَا لَمْ يَلْبَثُوٓا۟ إِلَّا عَشِيَّةً أَوْ ضُحَىٰهَا

claim: The word in 79:46 is ʿashiyya, not ʿaṣr, but the paragraph links them because al-ʿaṣr can also mean afternoon: seen from the end, a long era becomes like an evening.
The plea in 35:37 by the people in Hell to be brought out so they can do righteous deeds presents their request as work that came too late.
terms: رَبَّنَآ أَخْرِجْنَا نَعْمَلْ صَٰلِحًا غَيْرَ ٱلَّذِى كُنَّا نَعْمَلُ
rabbanā akhrijnā naʿmal ṣāliḥan ghayra alladhī kunnā naʿmal

claim: The answer in 35:37 says that they had been given a lifespan long enough for anyone who would reflect to take heed.
terms: أَوَلَمْ نُعَمِّرْكُم مَّا يَتَذَكَّرُ فِيهِ مَن تَذَكَّرَ
a-wa-lam nuʿammirkum mā yatadhakkaru fīhi man tadhakkar

claim: The loss stated in the surah’s second verse and the faith and righteous action stated in its third verse both fall within the lifespan that was given.
The images that follow are presented as accompanying the verse’s sense of time, not replacing it.
The root’s most concrete action is squeezing: pressing something until its liquid flows out.
A miʿṣār, like a feed bag, was used to hold and squeeze grapes, and a maʿṣara was the place where grapes were pressed.
terms: المعصار شيء كالمخلاة يجعل فيه العنب ويعصر

claim: In the described process, a bag holds the grapes while a hand or weight presses them, breaking their skins so liquid seeps through the fabric.
The liquid that runs off from pressing is called al-ʿuṣāra, and anything whose water has been squeezed out is called ʿaṣīr.
terms: كل شيء عصر ماؤه فهو عصير

claim: What remains in the bag after squeezing is pulp.
Squeezing divides a thing into a flowing essence and a dry mass left behind.
Arabic usage makes the expressed essence and the thing pressed a figure for goodness and generosity.
terms: العرب تجعل العصارة والمعتصر مثلا للخير والعطاء

claim: A generous person may be praised with the expression yaʿṣiru fīnā, meaning that he gives to us as you give.
The yield taken from land is also called al-ʿuṣāra.
Clouds are described as being squeezed by rain or as letting rain flow, and a group that receives rain may be described with the verb ʿuṣira.
The Qurʾan names these clouds al-muʿṣirāt in 78:14 and says that abundant water is sent down from them.
Verses 78:14–16 are read as a chain of blessing: squeezed clouds produce pouring water, then grain and plants, then lush gardens.
A tongue dried by thirst is called al-maʿṣūr, described as squeezed and left without water.
Iʿtiṣār names the act of someone choking on food and drinking water in small sips to help the morsel go down.
terms: الاعتصار أن يغص الإنسان بالطعام فيعتصر بالماء وهو أن يشربه قليلا قليلا ليسيغه

claim: The poem’s counterfactual suggests that the speaker is choked by water itself, leaving no sip of water to relieve the choking.
terms: لو بغير الماء حلقي شرق كنت كالغصان بالماء اعتصاري
law bi-ghayri al-māʾi ḥalqī shariqun kuntu ka-l-ghaṣṣāni bi-l-māʾi iʿtiṣārī

claim: Alongside the verse’s sense of time, these images make time appear as a pressure that passes over a person and draws something out of them.
What time draws out may flow as an essence, generosity, or rain, while what remains may be a dry mass or a tongue dried by thirst.
The loss in the surah’s second verse is identified with the leftover side of what has been squeezed.
The surah’s final word, ṣabr, is also the name of the bitter essence squeezed from a tree, carrying the image of pressure to the surah’s end.
The Qurʾan uses the verb for squeezing in a prison narrative and places that act within an extended wait.
After Yusuf’s innocence is clear, those deciding his fate send him to prison until a time; the verse measures the confinement as lasting for a period.
The paragraph connects the prison’s period of confinement to dictionary senses of ʿaṣr as a time span and as holding someone back, while noting that the Qurʾan uses a different word for prison.
One young man dreams that he is squeezing wine; the paragraph says the grapes are being pressed but the sentence names the action by its product, the wine.
Yusuf interprets the dream to mean that one of the young men will serve wine to his master, and the next verse identifies that man as the one expected to be saved.
The dictionary sense of al-ʿaṣr as a place of deliverance echoes here: the man who dreams of pressing wine is the one who gets out of prison.
The young man forgets Yusuf, who remains in prison for several years, as 12:42 recounts.
The cupbearer who escaped prison remembers Yusuf only after a long time, as 12:45 relates.
The king’s dream contains seven green ears of grain and seven others that are dry.
Yusuf interprets the dream as a plan: for seven years the people should sow and leave most of what they reap in its ear, eating only a little.
terms: فَمَا حَصَدتُّمْ فَذَرُوهُ فِى سُنۢبُلِهِۦٓ إِلَّا قَلِيلًۭا مِّمَّا تَأْكُلُونَ

claim: Arabic usage calls a crop ʿaṣara when the husks of its ears have appeared, and the expression is connected to ʿaṣr as protection because the grain is guarded in its husk.
terms: إذا تبينت أكمام السنبل قيل قد عصر الزرع
مأخوذ من العصر وهو الحرز أي تحرز في غلفه

claim: The paragraph treats this as an analogy of protected storage, while stressing that the Qurʾan’s word is the grain ear, not ʿaṣr: Yusuf’s plan keeps the grain inside its husk for the lean years.
After the seven good years come seven hard years that consume what was stored, leaving only a little of what was protected.
terms: ثُمَّ يَأْتِى مِنۢ بَعْدِ ذَٰلِكَ سَبْعٌۭ شِدَادٌۭ يَأْكُلْنَ مَا قَدَّمْتُمْ لَهُنَّ إِلَّا قَلِيلًۭا مِّمَّا تُحْصِنُونَ

claim: The final year brings relief to the people and is the year in which they squeeze.
terms: ثُمَّ يَأْتِى مِنۢ بَعْدِ ذَٰلِكَ عَامٌۭ فِيهِ يُغَاثُ ٱلنَّاسُ وَفِيهِ يَعْصِرُونَ
ʿāmun fīhi yughāthu al-nāsu wa-fīhi yaʿṣirūn

claim: The verb yaʿṣirūn in 12:49 is also understood to mean that people take produce from their lands.

The story arranges several distant senses of the root in a single calendar: prison time, squeezing in a dream, years prolonged by forgetting, grain protected in its husk, and squeezing again in the year of abundance.
Here squeezing marks the end of hardship, and the grapes to be pressed become the share of those who waited patiently through the lean years and stored their grain.
The time sworn by in 103:1 is presented not only as time that consumes, but also as time in which what is stored is protected until it can be pressed and flow.
Squeezing is treated as a kind of grasping that can work in either direction: it can hold something back or make it flow out.
Al-ʿaṣr can mean detention or restraint, and mā ʿaṣaraka asks what held someone back or prevented them.
A person who keeps their hand closed and does not give may be called ʿāṣir.
The root is used for a father withholding a child’s property and for taking back a gift one had given.
terms: يعتصر الوالد على ولده في ماله أي يمنعه إياه ويحبسه عنه
أعطيت فلانا عطية فاعتصرتها أي رجعت فيها

claim: The previously described generous giver is also described with this root.
The bag image explains the contrast: a hand that squeezes can give when something flows out or be miserly when it only holds, and the difference is whether anything leaves the palm.
A young woman at her first menstruation may be called al-muʿṣir because she is kept at home and given a protected place.
terms: المعصر ساعة تطمث أي تحيض لأنها تحبس في البيت يجعل لها عصرا

claim: The seed kept inside its husk is likewise held within a protective refuge.
In these cases, holding means protecting someone or something at a threshold.
The Qurʾan presents the fate of a garden’s produce as a test for people who deny the Prophet.
terms: إِنَّا بَلَوْنَٰهُمْ كَمَا بَلَوْنَآ أَصْحَٰبَ ٱلْجَنَّةِ
innā balawnāhum ka-mā balawnā aṣḥāba al-jannah

claim: The garden owners swear that they will harvest it in the morning and make no exception.
Their plan is to keep any poor person from entering and sharing the garden’s produce.
terms: أَن لَّا يَدْخُلَنَّهَا ٱلْيَوْمَ عَلَيْكُم مِّسْكِينٌۭ
an lā yadkhulannahā al-yawma ʿalaykum miskīn

claim: While the owners sleep, a visitation from their Lord passes over the garden, which is then found darkened and cut down.
terms: فَطَافَ عَلَيْهَا طَآئِفٌۭ مِّن رَّبِّكَ وَهُمْ نَآئِمُونَ

claim: When they see the garden, the owners first say that they have lost their way and then say that they have been deprived.
The produce they meant to hold back is no longer in their hands.
The garden owners swear without exception, whereas the oath in this surah is followed by a general judgment in verse 2 and an exception in verse 3.
Alongside the meaning of squeezing, the root also has the seemingly surprising meaning of refuge.
The root describes attaching oneself to something and holding firmly to it.
Al-ʿaṣr can mean a refuge; iʿtaṣartu bi-fulānin or taʿaṣṣartu means that one sought refuge with someone, and iʿtaṣara bi-l-makān means that one took refuge in a place.
terms: اعتصرت بفلان وتعصرت أي التجأت إليه

claim: The expression ʿuṣrat al-manjūd means a refuge for a distressed or tightly pressed person.
The saying mā baynahumā ʿaṣrun wa-lā yaṣr means that two people have neither affection nor kinship between them.
terms: ما بينهما عصر ولا يصر أي ما بينهما مودة ولا قرابة

claim: The root naṣara in the word ʿunṣur is said to mean origin and lineage, and the word’s origin is explained as ʿaṣr, meaning refuge, with an added nūn.
terms: العنصر أصل الحسب ومما زيدت فيه النون وهو في الأصل العصر وهو الملجأ

claim: Armor called al-maʿāṣir is derived from this root because a person is protected by it.
terms: المعاصر الدروع مأخوذ من العصر لأنه يعصر بها

claim: The paragraph resolves the apparent conflict between squeezing and refuge by treating both as forms of grasping.
Squeezing wraps around something from the outside, while the person seeking refuge grips something, and armor wraps around and protects the body.
The refuge in the expression for a distressed person is specifically a refuge for someone who is overwhelmed or pressed.
Heard alongside the meaning of time, the sworn-by period appears both as a span that presses people and as a place in which to seek refuge.
The cave story is used to show how a refuge can close off a person’s sense of time.
The youths separate from their people and what they worship besides God, then are told to take refuge in the cave so that God will spread His mercy over them.
terms: فَأْوُۥٓا۟ إِلَى ٱلْكَهْفِ يَنشُرْ لَكُمْ رَبُّكُم مِّن رَّحْمَتِهِۦ
faʾwū ilā al-kahfi yanshur lakum rabbukum min raḥmatihi

claim: When they take refuge in the cave, the youths pray for mercy from God.
terms: إِذْ أَوَى ٱلْفِتْيَةُ إِلَى ٱلْكَهْفِ فَقَالُوا۟ رَبَّنَآ ءَاتِنَا مِن لَّدُنكَ رَحْمَةًۭ
idh awā al-fityatu ilā al-kahfi fa-qālū rabbanā ātinā min ladunka raḥmah

claim: Inside the cave, God puts the youths to sleep for a counted number of years.
terms: فَضَرَبْنَا عَلَىٰٓ ءَاذَانِهِمْ فِى ٱلْكَهْفِ سِنِينَ عَدَدًۭا
fa-ḍarabnā ʿalā ādhānihim fī al-kahfi sinīna ʿadadā

claim: On waking, the youths think they stayed a day or part of a day, although the account says they remained in the cave three hundred years and nine more.
terms: وَلَبِثُوا۟ فِى كَهْفِهِمْ ثَلَٰثَ مِا۟ئَةٍۢ سِنِينَ وَٱزْدَادُوا۟ تِسْعًۭا

claim: Although the word al-ʿaṣr does not occur in this story, the paragraph hears three of its senses together: refuge, a long era, and a span that sleepers experience as only a moment.
The exception of believers in the surah’s third verse is linked to this refuge image, so escape from loss is heard here as taking refuge somewhere.
A branch of the root names a wind that rises into the sky.
An iʿṣār is a wind that raises dust into a column toward the sky, and the swirling rising dust itself is also called iʿṣār.
terms: الإعصار ريح تهب تثير الغبار فيرتفع إلى السماء كأنه عمود
الإعصار الغبار الذي يسطع مستديرا والجمع الأعاصير

claim: The wind’s motion gathers what is on the ground, turns it, and draws it upward as a vertical column.
The same root also describes fragrance rising behind a perfumed woman; al-ʿuṣra is the spreading and swelling of perfume.
terms: تكون العصرة من فوح الطيب وهيجه

claim: The root’s image is something moving and rising behind what has passed: dust in one case, fragrance in the other.
The Qurʾan places the whirlwind in a parable about a garden belonging to an old person, in the context of examples about spending in God’s way.
The example for someone who spends for show is a smooth rock covered in soil that a downpour leaves bare.
terms: فَمَثَلُهُۥ كَمَثَلِ صَفْوَانٍ عَلَيْهِ تُرَابٌۭ فَأَصَابَهُۥ وَابِلٌۭ فَتَرَكَهُۥ صَلْدًۭا
ṣafwān ʿalayhi turābun fa-aṣābahu wābilun fa-tarakahu ṣaldā

claim: The example for one who spends seeking God’s pleasure is a garden on a height that yields twice as much whether it receives heavy rain or drizzle.
The passage asks whether anyone would want a garden of date palms and grapes with rivers flowing beneath it.
terms: أَيَوَدُّ أَحَدُكُمْ أَن تَكُونَ لَهُۥ جَنَّةٌۭ مِّن نَّخِيلٍۢ وَأَعْنَابٍۢ تَجْرِى مِن تَحْتِهَا ٱلْأَنْهَٰرُ
a-yawaddu aḥadukum an takūna lahu jannatun min nakhīlin wa-aʿnābin

claim: The garden owner is struck by old age and has weak children when a whirlwind containing fire strikes the garden and burns it.
terms: وَأَصَابَهُ ٱلْكِبَرُ وَلَهُۥ ذُرِّيَّةٌۭ ضُعَفَآءُ فَأَصَابَهَآ إِعْصَارٌۭ فِيهِ نَارٌۭ فَٱحْتَرَقَتْ
aṣābahu al-kibaru wa-lahu dhurriyyatun ḍuʿafāʾu fa-aṣābahā iʿṣārun fīhi nārun fa-iḥtaraqat

claim: The verse concludes that God explains the signs so that people may reflect.
terms: كَذَٰلِكَ يُبَيِّنُ ٱللَّهُ لَكُمُ ٱلْءَايَٰتِ لَعَلَّكُمْ تَتَفَكَّرُونَ
kadhālika yubayyinu Allāhu lakumu al-āyāti laʿallakum tatafakkarūn

claim: Several root associations gather in the garden scene, but the only word from the root that appears there is iʿṣār, the whirlwind.
The garden has grapes, fruit to be squeezed; rivers and produce, a source of yield; and an owner who has reached old age, the evening of life.
A wind that lifts things from the ground and raises them skyward, now carrying fire, destroys the garden.
The owner loses the crop he had waited a lifetime to harvest at the point when he no longer has strength to plant again.
This garden is offered as the most concrete picture of the loss in 103:2, with the whirlwind showing how time can scatter what has been accumulated.
The rise of fragrance supplies the opposite possibility: after someone passes, a good trace rather than dust may remain.
